1.solution: The wavenumber of a hydrogen spectral line is \(\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n^2} - \frac{1}{m^2}\right)\). The "last line" (series limit) of a series corresponds to \(m \to \infty\). For the Lyman series \(n = 1\), so \(\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R\left(\frac{1}{1} - 0\right) = R\). For the Balmer series \(n = 2\), so \(\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - 0\right) = \frac{R}{4}\). Therefore \(\frac{\lambda_L}{\lambda_B} = \frac{R/4}{R} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25\).

2.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
2.solution: A perfectly black body absorbs all the radiation incident on it and is also the best possible emitter. By definition, its coefficient of emission (emissivity) is the maximum possible value, namely unity \((e = 1)\).

3.solution: Travel from A to B through the series elements. A current \(I = 2\,\text{A}\) flows from A. Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law and accounting for the drop across each element and the cell: \(V_A - I(2\,\Omega) - 3\,\text{V} - I(1\,\Omega) = V_B\). Here the potential falls by \(IR\) across each resistor in the direction of current and falls by 3 V across the cell (entering at + and leaving at -). Thus \(V_A - (2)(2) - 3 - (2)(1) = V_B\), giving \(V_A - V_B = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9\,\text{V}\).

4.subtopic: Newton's Laws — Force, Tension, Lift, and Connected Blocks
4.solution: An inertial frame of reference is one that moves with constant velocity (zero acceleration). A train slowing down, a child on a merry-go-round (circular motion), and an aeroplane taking off are all accelerating, hence non-inertial. Only the driver of a bus moving with constant velocity is in an inertial frame.

5.subtopic: Moment of Inertia, Theorems, and Radius of Gyration
5.solution: For a disc, \(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\) and \(M = \rho(\pi R^2 t)\) for same material (density \(\rho\)) and thickness \(t\). Hence \(I = \frac{1}{2}\rho \pi t R^4\), so \(I \propto R^4\). Therefore \(\frac{I_A}{I_B} = \frac{R^4}{(3R)^4} = \frac{1}{81}\), i.e. \(1:81\). The AK incorrectly used \(I \propto R^2\) (valid only for equal masses); here the masses differ because both discs are of the same material and thickness, so mass scales with \(R^2\) as well, giving the extra factor.
5.note: AK says B (1:9) using I ∝ R² for equal-mass discs. But the discs have the SAME material and thickness, so mass M = ρπR²t differs and I = ½MR² ∝ R⁴. Ratio = R⁴/(3R)⁴ = 1/81 = option C.

6.subtopic: Doppler Effect — Moving Source and Observer
6.solution: For a stationary source and a moving observer, the apparent frequency is \(F' = \left(\frac{v \pm V_1}{v}\right)F\), with + when approaching and - when receding. So \(F_1 = \frac{v + V_1}{v}F\) and \(F_2 = \frac{v - V_1}{v}F\). Then \(\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{v + V_1}{v - V_1} = 2\), giving \(v + V_1 = 2v - 2V_1\), so \(v = 3V_1\) and \(\frac{v}{V_1} = 3\).

7.solution: The reaction \(_{6}\text{C}^{11} \to {}_{5}\text{B}^{11} + \beta^{+} + X\) is a beta-plus (positron) decay: a proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron \(\beta^{+}\). To conserve lepton number and energy-momentum, a neutrino \((\nu)\) is emitted along with the positron. (Beta-minus decay emits an antineutrino; beta-plus decay emits a neutrino.) Hence \(X\) is a neutrino.

8.solution: In the fundamental mode of a pipe closed at one end, the air column length equals \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\). The time \(t\) given is for the wave to traverse this length \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\). The period of the wave (time to traverse one full wavelength \(\lambda\)) is therefore \(T = 4t\). The frequency is \(f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{4t} = (4t)^{-1}\).

9.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
9.solution: The wire has three sections. Sections (i) and (iii) are straight wires whose lines pass through (or are directed at) the centre O — a straight conductor produces zero magnetic field at points lying along its own line, so these contribute nothing at O. Section (ii) is a semicircle of radius R carrying current I. The field at the centre of a full circular loop is \(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\); for a semicircle it is half of this: \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}\).

10.solution: Mean time \(\bar{t} = \frac{30 + 32 + 35 + 35}{4} = \frac{132}{4} = 33\,\text{s}\). The absolute deviations are \(|30-33| = 3\), \(|32-33| = 1\), \(|35-33| = 2\), \(|35-33| = 2\). Mean absolute error \(\Delta t = \frac{3 + 1 + 2 + 2}{4} = \frac{8}{4} = 2\,\text{s}\). Hence the correct mean time is \((33 \pm 2)\,\text{s}\).

11.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
11.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect — Stopping Potential, Threshold, and Work Function
11.solution: Photoelectric emission occurs only when the photon energy is at least the work function: \(\frac{hc}{\lambda} \geq \frac{hc}{\lambda_0}\). This requires \(\frac{1}{\lambda} \geq \frac{1}{\lambda_0}\), i.e. \(\lambda \leq \lambda_0\). The incident wavelength must not exceed the threshold wavelength.

12.subtopic: Circular Motion — Angular Velocity, Centripetal Force, Vertical Circle
12.solution: In uniform circular motion (constant angular speed) the velocity is tangential, the centripetal acceleration points toward the centre, and velocity and acceleration are mutually perpendicular. Hence statements A, C and D are true. The false statement is that the acceleration vector is tangent to the circle — it is in fact directed toward the centre, not tangential.

13.subtopic: Young's Double Slit, Biprism, and Interference
13.solution: Introducing a thin glass plate of thickness \(t\) and refractive index \(\mu\) over one slit shifts the fringe pattern by \(\Delta y = \frac{(\mu - 1)tD}{d}\), where \(D\) is the screen distance and \(d\) the slit separation. Substituting \(t = 0.04\,\text{mm} = 0.04 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), \(\mu = 1.5\), \(D = 1\,\text{m}\), \(d = 2\,\text{mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\): \(\Delta y = \frac{(0.5)(0.04 \times 10^{-3})(1)}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.01\,\text{m} = 1\,\text{cm}\).
13.note: Stem calls d=2mm the 'slit width' but it is the slit separation (distance between slits), consistent with the AK calculation.

14.subtopic: p-n Junction Diode — Biasing, I-V, and Rectifiers
14.solution: An ideal diode behaves as a perfect conductor when forward biased (zero resistance) and as a perfect insulator when reverse biased (infinite resistance). Hence the resistances are zero (forward) and infinite (reverse).

15.subtopic: Young's Double Slit, Biprism, and Interference
15.solution: The number of fringes covering a fixed region of the screen is inversely proportional to wavelength, since fringe width \(\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}\). For a fixed width \(W\), \(n = \frac{W}{\beta} \propto \frac{1}{\lambda}\), so \(n_1 \lambda_1 = n_2 \lambda_2\). Thus \(18 \times 600 = n_2 \times 400\), giving \(n_2 = \frac{10800}{400} = 27\).

16.solution: First \(\vec{P} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C} = (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) + (-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+4\hat{k}) + (2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-8\hat{k}) = 2\hat{i} - \hat{k}\). Next \(\vec{Q} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \hat{i}(1\cdot4 - 3\cdot1) - \hat{j}(1\cdot4 - 3\cdot(-1)) + \hat{k}(1\cdot1 - 1\cdot(-1)) = \hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). The dot product \(\vec{P}\cdot\vec{Q} = (2)(1) + (0)(-7) + (-1)(2) = 2 - 2 = 0\). Since \(\vec{P}\cdot\vec{Q} = 0\), the angle between them is \(90^\circ\). (Indeed \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\); here \(\vec{P}\) happens to lie in their plane.)

17.subtopic: Reactance — Inductive, Capacitive, and Single-Element Circuits
17.solution: The bulb's brightness depends on the current, which is reduced when the circuit impedance rises. Inserting an iron rod into the coil increases its inductance \(L\), hence increases the inductive reactance \(X_L = 2\pi f L\) and the impedance, reducing the current and dimming the bulb. Reducing frequency or turns, or adding capacitance to reduce net reactance, would each increase current (brighten the bulb). Hence the brightness decreases when an iron rod is inserted.

18.subtopic: SHM Kinematics — Displacement, Velocity, Phase, and Damping
18.solution: Phase is \(\phi = \omega t = \frac{2\pi}{T}t\). With \(T = 16\,\text{s}\): at \(t = 2\,\text{s}\), \(\phi_1 = \frac{2\pi}{16}(2) = \frac{\pi}{4}\); at \(t = 4\,\text{s}\), \(\phi_2 = \frac{2\pi}{16}(4) = \frac{\pi}{2}\). The phase difference is \(\Delta\phi = \phi_2 - \phi_1 = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}\).

19.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
19.solution: By Newton's law of cooling, \(\frac{\theta_1 - \theta_2}{t} = K\left(\frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2} - \theta_0\right)\). First interval: \(\frac{60 - 40}{6} = K\left(\frac{60+40}{2} - 10\right) = K(40)\), so \(K = \frac{20}{6 \times 40} = \frac{1}{12}\). Second interval (final temperature \(x\)): \(\frac{40 - x}{6} = \frac{1}{12}\left(\frac{40 + x}{2} - 10\right)\). Multiplying out: \(40 - x = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{40+x}{2} - 10\right)\) \(\Rightarrow 4(40 - x) = (40 + x) - 20 \Rightarrow 160 - 4x = 20 + x \Rightarrow 5x = 140 \Rightarrow x = 28^\circ\text{C}\).

20.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
20.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect — Stopping Potential, Threshold, and Work Function
20.solution: Radiation pressure: an absorbed beam of power \(P_a\) exerts force \(\frac{P_a}{c}\); a reflected beam of power \(P_r\) exerts force \(\frac{2P_r}{c}\). Here total \(P = 90\,\text{W}\), with 50% absorbed \((P_a = 45\,\text{W})\) and 50% reflected \((P_r = 45\,\text{W})\). Total force \(F = \frac{P_a}{c} + \frac{2P_r}{c} = \frac{45 + 90}{3 \times 10^8} = \frac{135}{3 \times 10^8} = 4.5 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{N}\).

21.subtopic: Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Equation
21.solution: At constant volume, Gay-Lussac's law gives \(\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}\). With \(P_1 = 270\,\text{kPa}\), \(T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\,\text{K}\), \(T_2 = 37 + 273 = 310\,\text{K}\): \(P_2 = P_1\frac{T_2}{T_1} = 270 \times \frac{310}{300} = 279\,\text{kPa}\).

22.subtopic: Series LCR — Impedance, Phase, and Resonance
22.solution: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit is \(f_r = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\), which depends only on \(L\) and \(C\) and is independent of the resistance \(R\). Changing \(R\) to one-third its value does not alter \(f_r\), so the resonant frequency remains unchanged.

23.solution: For a spring-mass system \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\), so \(T \propto \sqrt{m}\). Hence \(\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \sqrt{\frac{4m}{m}} = 2\), giving \(T_2 = 2 \times 2 = 4\,\text{s}\).

24.subtopic: Self-Inductance, Energy Stored, and LR Circuit
24.solution: The induced e.m.f. in an inductor is \(e = -L\frac{dI}{dt}\). Since \(L\) is constant, \(e\) is directly proportional to \(\frac{dI}{dt}\) — i.e. the graph of \(e\) versus \(\frac{dI}{dt}\) is a straight line passing through the origin (with negative slope, the magnitude of \(e\) increasing linearly with \(\frac{dI}{dt}\)). The correct option is the figure showing this straight-line variation through the origin.
24.note: The four images are the answer-option figures (graphs labelled A/B/C/D in the stem; parsed option letters remap to those figure labels). Correct physics: e ∝ dI/dt, a straight line through origin. Kept AK answer B; figures attached as images.

25.solution: The total electrostatic potential energy of three charges \(+Q\), \(+2Q\) and \(q\) at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \(r\) is \(U = \frac{k}{r}\big[(Q)(2Q) + (Q)(q) + (2Q)(q)\big]\). Setting \(U = 0\): \(2Q^2 + Qq + 2Qq = 0\), i.e. \(2Q^2 + 3Qq = 0\). Dividing by \(Q\): \(2Q + 3q = 0\), so \(q = -\frac{2}{3}Q\).

26.subtopic: Surface Tension, Surface Energy, and Capillary Rise
26.solution: Conserving volume, a big drop of radius \(R\) splitting into \(n\) droplets of radius \(r\) gives \(R^3 = n r^3\), so \(r = R n^{-1/3}\). With \(n = 1000\), \(r = \frac{R}{10}\). Surface energy = surface tension \(\times\) area. Original: \(V = T(4\pi R^2)\). Total of droplets: \(V' = n \cdot T(4\pi r^2) = 1000 \cdot T \cdot 4\pi \frac{R^2}{100} = 10 \cdot T(4\pi R^2) = 10V\).

27.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain
27.solution: In a common-emitter amplifier, the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased; the input impedance is low and output impedance high; and the input and output voltages are out of phase by \(180^\circ\). The correct statement is that the input signal is applied between base and emitter and the output is taken between collector and emitter.

28.subtopic: Kinetic Theory — Pressure, RMS Speed, and Temperature
28.solution: The average force on the walls relates to pressure by \(F = PA\), so \(F \propto P\) for a fixed wall area. For an ideal gas at constant volume, \(P = \frac{nRT}{V} \propto T\). Hence \(F \propto T\), i.e. \(F \propto T^x\) with \(x = 1\).

29.solution: By Gauss's law, the total flux through the closed cylinder is \(\phi_A + \phi_B + \phi_C = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\), where A and C are the two plane (flat) end surfaces and B is the curved surface with flux \(\phi\). By symmetry the two flat ends carry equal flux, \(\phi_A = \phi_C\). Thus \(2\phi_A + \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\), giving \(\phi_A = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} - \phi\right)\).

30.subtopic: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric, and Isochoric Processes
30.solution: For an adiabatic process, \(TV^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}\). Hence \(T_i V_0^{\gamma-1} = T_f \left(\frac{V_0}{32}\right)^{\gamma-1}\), giving \(\frac{T_f}{T_i} = 32^{\gamma - 1} = 32^{7/5 - 1} = 32^{2/5}\). Since \(32 = 2^5\), \(32^{2/5} = 2^2 = 4\). With \(T_f = xT_i\), \(x = 4\).

31.solution: The e.m.f. induced in the secondary is \(e_s = M\frac{dI_p}{dt}\). Solving for time: \(dt = \frac{M \, dI_p}{e_s} = \frac{(2)(6 - 3)}{2 \times 10^3} = \frac{6}{2000} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s}\).

32.subtopic: Surface Tension, Surface Energy, and Capillary Rise
32.solution: Conserving volume, \(R^3 = n r^3\) with \(n = 729\), so \(r = \frac{R}{9}\) (since \(729 = 9^3\)). Surface energy scales with surface area: original \(E = T(4\pi R^2)\); total of droplets \(E' = n \cdot T(4\pi r^2) = 729 \cdot T \cdot 4\pi \frac{R^2}{81} = 9 \cdot T(4\pi R^2) = 9E\).

33.subtopic: Gravitational PE, Escape Velocity, and Energy
33.solution: For a body projected upward with speed \(v\), energy conservation gives the maximum height \(h = \frac{R}{(v_e/v)^2 - 1}\), where \(v_e\) is escape velocity. With \(v = \frac{v_e}{3}\), \(\frac{v_e}{v} = 3\), so \(h = \frac{R}{9 - 1} = \frac{R}{8}\).

34.solution: The current \(I\) flows in the larger ring of radius \(r_1\), producing at the common centre a nearly uniform field \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1}\) over the small inner ring of radius \(r_2\). The flux linked with the small ring is \(\phi = B \cdot \pi r_2^2 = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2 r_1} I\). The mutual inductance is \(M = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2 r_1}\). Among the given options, the correct form is \(\frac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2 r_1}\) where the numerator radius is the smaller ring; option B reads \(\frac{\mu_0 \pi r_1^2}{2 r_1}\) but is the intended correct choice (the inner radius in the numerator should be \(r_2\); the printed option has a typo).
34.note: Correct M = μ₀πr₂²/(2r₁). Printed option B reads μ₀πr₁²/(2r₁) — a printed typo (should be r₂² in numerator). It is still the intended/closest correct option; AK answer B kept. Option A (μ₀πr₁²/2r₂) is structurally wrong (large radius in numerator, small in denominator).

35.subtopic: First Law, Internal Energy, and Work-Heat Relations
35.solution: The work done in a cyclic process equals the area enclosed by the loop on the P-V diagram, with sign set by the sense of traversal. The cycle is the triangle ABC with the horizontal base \(AB\) of length \((3V - V) = 2V\) and height \((4P - P) = 3P\). Area \(= \frac{1}{2}(2V)(3P) = 3PV\). The cycle is traversed anticlockwise (A to B to C and back), so the net work done by the gas is negative: \(W = -3PV\). The intended correct option is \(-3PV\) (printed as "-3 v").
35.note: Option D is printed as '-3 v', a truncation of '-3 PV'. The intended answer is -3PV; AK answer D kept.

36.solution: Inside a charged conducting sphere the electric field is zero everywhere (the charge resides on the surface). The potential inside a conductor is constant and equals the surface potential, \(V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}\). Hence at the centre the field is zero and the potential is \(\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}\).

37.subtopic: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Rolling Motion
37.solution: For a body rolling down an incline without slipping, \(a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2}}\). For a solid sphere \(\frac{K^2}{R^2} = \frac{2}{5}\), so \(a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{2}{5}} = \frac{5g\sin\theta}{7}\). With \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\sin\theta = 0.5\): \(a = \frac{5g}{7}(0.5) = \frac{5g}{14}\).

38.solution: For an open pipe the fundamental frequency is \(f = \frac{v}{2L}\), so \(L = \frac{v}{2f}\). For the two pipes, \(L_1 = \frac{v}{2f_1}\) and \(L_2 = \frac{v}{2f_2}\). Joined in series the effective open pipe has length \(L = L_1 + L_2\), with fundamental \(f = \frac{v}{2L}\). Hence \(\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}\), giving \(f = \frac{f_1 f_2}{f_1 + f_2}\).

39.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
39.solution: A wire of fixed total length \(\ell\) bent into one turn of radius \(r\) gives \(\ell = 2\pi r\) and field \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}\). When bent into \(n\) turns, each turn has radius \(r' = \frac{r}{n}\) (same total length). The field at the centre is \(B_n = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2r'} = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2(r/n)} = n^2 \cdot \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r} = n^2 B\).

40.subtopic: Moment of Inertia, Theorems, and Radius of Gyration
40.solution: The axis passes through the centre of sphere 1, perpendicular to the rod. Sphere 1 rotates about its own diameter: \(I_1 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2\). Sphere 2's centre is at distance equal to its own radius + rod length + radius of sphere 1... here the centres are separated by the rod length \(4R\) (the rod connects the two sphere surfaces? Using the figure, centre-to-centre distance is \(4R\)). By the parallel-axis theorem, \(I_2 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + M(4R)^2 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + 16MR^2\). The rod is massless. Total: \(I = I_1 + I_2 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + 16MR^2 = \frac{4}{5}MR^2 + \frac{80}{5}MR^2 = \frac{84}{5}MR^2\).

41.subtopic: Young's Double Slit, Biprism, and Interference
41.solution: Destructive interference (a dark fringe) requires the path difference to be an odd multiple of half a wavelength, i.e. a phase difference that is an odd multiple of \(\pi\). For the \(n\)th dark fringe \((n = 1,2,3,\ldots)\) the phase difference is \(\Delta\phi = (2n - 1)\pi\).

42.subtopic: Surface Tension, Surface Energy, and Capillary Rise
42.solution: The volume of water is \(V = 0.01\,\text{cm}^3\) and it spreads over area \(A = 10\,\text{cm}^2\) (the stem prints '0 cm^2' — a dropped digit; the AK uses 10 cm^2). The film thickness is \(d = \frac{V}{A}\). The normal force to separate the plates is \(F = \frac{2TA}{d} = \frac{2TA^2}{V}\). Substituting \(T = 70\,\text{dyne/cm}\), \(A = 10\,\text{cm}^2\), \(V = 0.01\,\text{cm}^3\): \(F = \frac{2(70)(10)^2}{0.01} = \frac{14000}{0.01} = 1.4 \times 10^6\,\text{dyne} = 14\,\text{N}\).
42.stemOverride: A water drop of \(0.01\,\text{cm}^3\) is squeezed between two glass plates and spreads into an area of \(10\,\text{cm}^2\). If surface tension of water is 70 dyne/cm, then the normal force required to separate the glass plates from each other will be

43.solution: The internal resistance via the potentiometer shunt method is \(r = R\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)\), where \(l_1\) is the balancing length with the cell open (unshunted) and \(l_2\) with shunt \(R\). With \(R = 5\,\Omega\), \(l_2 = 200\,\text{cm}\): \(r = 5\left(\frac{l_1}{200} - 1\right)\). With \(R = 15\,\Omega\), \(l_2 = 300\,\text{cm}\): \(r = 15\left(\frac{l_1}{300} - 1\right)\). Equating: \(5\left(\frac{l_1}{200} - 1\right) = 15\left(\frac{l_1}{300} - 1\right) \Rightarrow \frac{l_1}{40} - 5 = \frac{l_1}{20} - 15 \Rightarrow 10 = \frac{l_1}{20} - \frac{l_1}{40} = \frac{l_1}{40} \Rightarrow l_1 = 400\,\text{cm}\). Then \(r = 5\left(\frac{400}{200} - 1\right) = 5(1) = 5\,\Omega\).

44.subtopic: Series LCR — Impedance, Phase, and Resonance
44.solution: Inductive reactance \(X_L = 2\pi f L = 2\pi (100)\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right) = 100\,\Omega\). The phase angle between voltage and current in a series RL circuit is \(\tan\phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = \frac{100}{200} = 0.5\). Hence \(\phi = \tan^{-1}(0.5)\).

45.solution: The fundamental frequency of a wire is \(n = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{m'}}\), where linear mass density \(m' = \rho \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \propto \rho d^2\). Thus \(n = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4}}} = \frac{1}{L d}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\pi\rho}}\). So \(n \propto \frac{1}{L d}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho}}\). Taking the ratio with \(L_B = 2L\), \(T_B = 2T\), \(\rho_B = 2\rho\), \(d_B = 3d\): \(\frac{n_B}{n_A} = \frac{L_A d_A}{L_B d_B}\sqrt{\frac{T_B \rho_A}{T_A \rho_B}} = \frac{L \cdot d}{2L \cdot 3d}\sqrt{\frac{2T \cdot \rho}{T \cdot 2\rho}} = \frac{1}{6}\sqrt{1} = \frac{1}{6}\). Hence \(n_B : n_A = 1 : 6\).

46.solution: Potential of a charged sphere is \(V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}\). When \(n\) small drops, each of charge \(q\) and radius \(r\), coalesce into a big drop: charge \(q' = nq\) and (by volume conservation) radius \(r' = n^{1/3} r\). The new potential is \(V' = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{nq}{n^{1/3} r} = n^{2/3}\left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}\right) = n^{2/3} V\).

47.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain
47.solution: In a transistor, power gain = voltage gain \(\times\) current gain. Therefore \(\frac{\text{power gain}}{\text{voltage gain}} = \text{current gain}\). In the common-emitter configuration the current gain is \(\beta\). Hence the ratio equals \(\beta\).

48.subtopic: SHM Kinematics — Displacement, Velocity, Phase, and Damping
48.solution: Starting from the mean position, \(x = A\sin\omega t\) with \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\,\text{rad/s}\). Position at \(t = 1\,\text{s}\): \(x_1 = A\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\). Position at \(t = 2\,\text{s}\): \(x_2 = A\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = A\). Distance in the 1st second \(= x_1 = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\). Distance in the 2nd second \(= x_2 - x_1 = A - \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}} = A\frac{\sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2}}\). The ratio is \(\frac{x_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{A/\sqrt{2}}{A(\sqrt{2}-1)/\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} - 1}\), i.e. \(1 : (\sqrt{2} - 1)\).

49.solution: For a compound microscope at relaxed-eye (normal) adjustment, the tube length \(L = v_0 + f_e\), where \(v_0\) is the objective image distance and \(f_e\) the eyepiece focal length. So \(15 = v_0 + 6 \Rightarrow v_0 = 9\,\text{cm}\). The magnifying power for relaxed eye is \(m = \frac{v_0}{u_0}\cdot\frac{D}{f_e}\) with \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\). Thus \(25 = \frac{9}{u_0}\cdot\frac{25}{6}\), giving \(u_0 = \frac{9 \times 25}{25 \times 6} = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5\,\text{cm}\).

50.subtopic: Magnetisation, Susceptibility, Permeability, and B-H-M Relations
50.solution: The relative permeability is related to the magnetic susceptibility by \(\mu_r = 1 + \chi\). With \(\chi = 5499\): \(\mu_r = 1 + 5499 = 5500\).

51.solution: For \(\text{Ca}_{3}(\text{PO}_{4})_{2} \rightleftharpoons 3\,\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\,\text{PO}_{4}^{3-}\). If solubility is \(S\), then \([\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 3S\) and \([\text{PO}_{4}^{3-}] = 2S\). \(K_{sp} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}]^{3}[\text{PO}_{4}^{3-}]^{2} = (3S)^{3}(2S)^{2} = 27 \times 4 \times S^{5} = 108\,S^{5}\). Matches option B.

52.solution: The Gattermann-Koch formylation introduces a \(-\text{CHO}\) group onto an arene using carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in the presence of anhydrous \(\text{AlCl}_{3}\) (often with \(\text{CuCl}\)). Thus the reagent is \(\text{CO},\text{HCl}\) / anhydrous \(\text{AlCl}_{3}\). Matches option B.

53.subtopic: Batteries, Primary, Secondary and Fuel Cells
53.solution: In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell the species that gets oxidised at the anode acts as the reducing agent. At the anode: \(\text{H}_{2} + 2\,\text{OH}^{-} \longrightarrow 2\,\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + 2e^{-}\). Here \(\text{H}_{2}\) loses electrons (is oxidised), so \(\text{H}_{2}\) is the reducing agent. \(\text{O}_{2}\) is reduced at the cathode (it is the oxidising agent), and \(\text{NaOH}\) is only the electrolyte. The correct answer is \(\text{H}_{2}\), option A.
53.note: AK keys D (NaOH), which is wrong — NaOH is merely the electrolyte. The reducing agent is the species oxidised at the anode, which is H2 (option A).

54.subtopic: Temperature Dependence, Arrhenius and Collision Theory

55.subtopic: Reactions of Alkanes, Free Radical Halogenation
55.solution: Free-radical halogenation of propane (\(\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}\)) under UV light favours abstraction of the more stable secondary hydrogen. Substitution at the central (C-2) carbon predominates, giving 2-bromopropane. Matches option B.

56.solution: Butanenitrile is \(\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}\) (4 carbons including the nitrile carbon), so it forms from a 3-carbon alkyl halide via nucleophilic substitution by cyanide: \(\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl} + \text{KCN (alc.)} \longrightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN} + \text{KCl}\). The pair is n-propyl chloride and alcoholic KCN. Matches option D.
56.note: Reaction is preparation of a nitrile (precursor to amines); classified under Amines > Preparation since cyanide route is studied there.

57.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
57.solution: Reduction: \(\text{Zn}^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \longrightarrow \text{Zn}_{(s)}\), \(E^{\circ} = -0.76\,\text{V}\). Reversing it (oxidation) changes the sign: \(\text{Zn}_{(s)} \longrightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^{-}\), \(E^{\circ} = +0.76\,\text{V}\). Standard potential is an intensive property — multiplying the equation by 2 does NOT change \(E^{\circ}\). Hence for \(2\,\text{Zn}_{(s)} \longrightarrow 2\,\text{Zn}^{2+}_{(aq)} + 4e^{-}\), \(E^{\circ} = +0.76\,\text{V}\). Matches option D.

58.solution: Cisplatin is \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_{3})_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}]\). Its ligands are two ammonia (\(\text{NH}_{3}\)) molecules and two chloride (\(\text{Cl}^{-}\)) ions. Matches option B.

59.solution: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (A true), exhibits only the \(-1\) oxidation state (B true), and forms only one oxoacid, HOF (D true). However, fluorine has an anomalously LOW bond dissociation enthalpy (due to electron–electron repulsion between the small F atoms' lone pairs); chlorine has the highest among the halogens. So statement C ('high bond dissociation enthalpy among all halogens') is false. Matches option C.

60.subtopic: First Law of Thermodynamics, Internal Energy and Work
60.solution: Pressure-volume work is \(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V\). In a free expansion the gas expands into vacuum, so the external (opposing) pressure \(P_{ext} = 0\), giving \(W = 0\). The other processes (isobaric, adiabatic compression, isothermal expansion) all involve non-zero work. Matches option D.

61.subtopic: First Law of Thermodynamics, Internal Energy and Work
61.solution: \(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V\), so \(P_{ext} = -\dfrac{W}{V_{2}-V_{1}} = -\dfrac{(-600\,\text{J})}{(20-15)\,\text{dm}^{3}} = \dfrac{600\,\text{J}}{5\,\text{dm}^{3}} = 120\,\text{J dm}^{-3}\). Using \(1\,\text{bar dm}^{3} = 100\,\text{J}\): \(P_{ext} = \dfrac{120}{100} = 1.2\,\text{bar}\). Matches option A.

62.solution: Oxidation of glucose with bromine water gives gluconic acid (a monocarboxylic acid). Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises only the aldehyde (\(-\text{CHO}\)) group to \(-\text{COOH}\), confirming the presence of an aldehydic group. Oxime formation (A) confirms a carbonyl in general; acetate (D) confirms hydroxyl groups; saccharic acid (C, with conc. \(\text{HNO}_{3}\)) indicates a primary alcohol plus aldehyde. The specific aldehyde test is gluconic-acid formation with \(\text{Br}_{2}\) water. Matches option B.

63.solution: In \(\text{Na}_{2}\text{S}_{4}\text{O}_{6}\), Na has the integral oxidation state \(+1\). In \(\text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4}\), \(\text{Mn}_{3}\text{O}_{4}\) and \(\text{Pb}_{3}\text{O}_{4}\) the metal carries an average (fractional) oxidation state of \(+\tfrac{8}{3}\). So the metal is NOT in a fractional state in \(\text{Na}_{2}\text{S}_{4}\text{O}_{6}\). Matches option D.

64.subtopic: Nomenclature and Classification of Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
64.solution: Adipic acid (hexanedioic), glutaric acid (pentanedioic) and malonic acid (propanedioic) are all dicarboxylic acids (two \(-\text{COOH}\) groups). Valeric acid is pentanoic acid, a monocarboxylic acid. Hence valeric acid is NOT a dicarboxylic acid. Matches option C.

65.solution: In the industrial (cumene) process, isopropylbenzene (cumene) is oxidised by air in the presence of cobalt naphthenate to cumene hydroperoxide, which on hydrolysis with dilute HCl gives phenol and acetone. Hence substrate X is isopropyl benzene (cumene). Matches option D.

66.solution: Glyptal is a polyester formed by condensation of ethylene glycol with phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid). (Terephthalic acid + ethylene glycol gives PET/dacron, not glyptal.) Hence the monomers are ethylene glycol and phthalic acid. Matches option D.

67.subtopic: Preparation of Alkanes, Wurtz, Grignard and Decarboxylation
67.solution: Ethanol \(\xrightarrow{\text{SOCl}_{2}}\) ethyl chloride (X) \(\xrightarrow{\text{Mg / dry ether}}\) ethyl magnesium chloride (Y, a Grignard reagent) \(\xrightarrow{\text{NH}_{3}}\) ethane (Z). A Grignard reagent reacts with a compound bearing an active hydrogen (here \(\text{NH}_{3}\)) to give the corresponding alkane: \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{MgCl} + \text{NH}_{3} \longrightarrow \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6} + \text{Mg(NH}_{2})\text{Cl}\). So Z is ethane. Matches option D.

68.subtopic: Enthalpy and Relation Between ΔH and ΔU
68.solution: Molar mass of ethanol \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} = 46\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\). Moles vaporised \(= \dfrac{11.5}{46} = 0.25\,\text{mol}\). Enthalpy of vaporisation \(= \dfrac{\text{heat supplied}}{\text{moles}} = \dfrac{11.8\,\text{kJ}}{0.25\,\text{mol}} = 47.2\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Matches option B.

69.subtopic: Diazonium Salts and Aromatic Amine Reactions
69.solution: The Sandmeyer reaction converts an aryl diazonium salt into an aryl halide or nitrile using cuprous salts: \(\text{CuCl}/\text{HCl}\), \(\text{CuBr}/\text{HBr}\), or \(\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}\). Among the options, \(\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}\) (giving aryl nitrile) is a Sandmeyer reagent. Matches option A.

70.solution: For \(\text{AgBr}_{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^{+}_{(aq)} + \text{Br}^{-}_{(aq)}\), \(K_{sp} = S^{2}\). With \(S = 7.1 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}\): \(K_{sp} = (7.1 \times 10^{-7})^{2} = 5.04 \times 10^{-13}\). Matches option D.
70.note: Stem solubility extracted as '.1 x 10^-7' (corrupted); true value is 7.1 x 10^-7 mol/dm^3, which yields the keyed answer 5.04 x 10^-13.
70.stemOverride: The solubility of AgBr is \(7.1 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate its solubility product at the same temperature.

71.subtopic: Carboxylic Acids, Properties, Reactions and Derivatives
71.solution: Methyl propanoate \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOCH}_{3}\) on hydrolysis with dilute \(\text{NaOH}\) gives sodium propanoate \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COONa}\) (A). Acidification of the sodium salt with conc. \(\text{HCl}\) liberates propanoic acid \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}\) (B). So B is propanoic acid. Matches option D.

72.subtopic: IUPAC Nomenclature, Functional Groups and Homologous Series
72.solution: In IUPAC seniority for the principal characteristic group, carboxylic acid derivatives rank highest among these: amide (\(-\text{CONH}_{2}\)) > nitrile (\(-\text{CN}\)) > amine (\(-\text{NH}_{2}\)); the C\(\equiv\)C triple bond is not a 'group' cited as a suffix-priority functional group above amide. Hence \(-\text{CONH}_{2}\) has the highest priority among the given groups. Matches option B.

73.solution: Sodium ethoxide is a strong, bulky base. With a secondary alkyl halide (isopropyl chloride) it favours E2 elimination over substitution, giving propene: \(\text{(CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCl} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{ONa} \longrightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=\text{CH}_{2} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} + \text{NaCl}\). So X is propene. Matches option C.

74.solution: A benzylic halide has the halogen on the carbon directly attached to the benzene ring. Triphenylmethane bears benzylic C-H positions; 1-bromo-1-phenylethane (\(\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}\)) and 2-bromo-2-phenylpropane (\(\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CBr(CH}_{3})_{2}\)) have Br on the benzylic carbon. In 1-bromo-2-phenylbutane the Br is on C-1 while the phenyl is on C-2, so the halogen-bearing carbon is NOT attached to the ring — it is a simple primary alkyl halide, not benzylic. Matches option D.

75.subtopic: Real Gases, Dalton's Law and KTG
75.solution: Compressibility factor \(Z = \dfrac{V_{\text{real}}}{V_{\text{ideal}}}\). At STP \(V_{\text{ideal}} = 22.4\,\text{dm}^{3}\), so \(V_{\text{real}} = Z \times 22.4 = 1.05 \times 22.4 = 23.52\,\text{dm}^{3}\). Matches option C.

76.subtopic: Crystal Defects, Magnetic Properties and Semiconductors
76.solution: Stainless steel is an interstitial alloy in which small carbon atoms occupy the interstitial sites between the larger iron atoms. This is an interstitial impurity defect. Matches option B.

77.subtopic: Inner Transition Elements, Lanthanoids and Actinoids
77.solution: Erbium (Er, Z = 68) belongs to the lanthanoid series (4f). Americium (Am), Neptunium (Np) and Lawrencium (Lr) are actinoids (5f). Hence the lanthanoid is Er. Matches option A.

78.subtopic: Batteries, Primary, Secondary and Fuel Cells
78.solution: \(\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\), so \(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -\dfrac{\Delta G^{\circ}}{nF}\). In a dry (Leclanché) cell the anode reaction \(\text{Zn} \longrightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+} + 2e^{-}\) transfers \(n = 2\) electrons. Hence \(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -\dfrac{\Delta G^{\circ}}{2F}\). Matches option B.

79.solution: Freezing-point depression \(\Delta T_{f} = i\,K_{f}\,m\) depends on the total particle concentration \(i\,m\). Computing effective particle molality: 0.1 m NaCl \(\to\) 0.2 m; 0.05 m \(\text{MgSO}_{4}\) \(\to\) 0.1 m; 0.05 m \(\text{Al}_{2}(\text{SO}_{4})_{3}\) \(\to\) \(0.05 \times 5 = 0.25\) m; 1 m \(\text{AlPO}_{4}\) \(\to\) \(1 \times 2 = 2\) m. The largest is 1 m \(\text{AlPO}_{4}\), so it shows the highest freezing point depression. Matches option C.

80.solution: For a hydrogen-like species, \(E_{n} = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\dfrac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\,\text{J}\). For \(\text{He}^{+}\), \(Z = 2\), \(n = 3\): \(E_{3} = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \dfrac{4}{9} = -9.69 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\). Matches option D.

82.solution: Te (group 16) has 6 valence electrons; in \(\text{TeF}_{4}\) four are used in bonding to four F atoms, leaving one lone pair. This is an \(\text{AB}_{4}\text{E}\) type with 5 electron domains, so the electron-pair (parent) geometry is trigonal bipyramidal (the molecular shape being see-saw). Among the options, the geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. Matches option C.
82.note: The actual molecular SHAPE of TeF4 is see-saw; the keyed 'trigonal bipyramidal' is the parent electron-domain geometry, which is the only consistent option given.

83.subtopic: Elements of Group 13, 14 and 15, Properties and Reactions
83.solution: Apatite is a calcium phosphate mineral, \(\text{Ca}_{5}(\text{PO}_{4})_{3}(\text{F},\text{Cl},\text{OH})\) (fluorapatite etc.), essentially containing Ca, P and O. Hence the set is Ca, P and O. Matches option B.
83.note: Phosphorus mineral; classified under p-block Group 15 (phosphorus chemistry).

84.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
84.solution: Negatively charged sols include \(\text{As}_{2}\text{S}_{3}\) sol, clay sol and congo red sol. Haemoglobin forms a positively charged sol. Hence the one that is NOT negatively charged is haemoglobin. Matches option B.

85.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life
85.solution: The unit of the rate constant indicates the order: for a first-order reaction the rate constant has units of (time)\(^{-1}\), i.e. \(\text{s}^{-1}\). The given \(k\) has units \(\text{s}^{-1}\), so the reaction is first order (order = 1). Matches option B.

86.solution: Thermoplastic polymers soften on heating and can be remoulded (linear/branched chains), e.g. polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Bakelite is a thermosetting (cross-linked) polymer. Hence the thermoplastic is polyvinyl. Matches option A.

87.subtopic: Position, Electronic Configuration and General Features of d-Block
87.solution: Ti (Z = 22): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{2}4s^{2}\). For \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\), remove three electrons (two 4s and one 3d): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{1}\). A single 3d electron means 1 unpaired electron. Matches option C.

88.solution: Number of atoms in 0.6 mol \(= 0.6 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.613 \times 10^{23}\). In hcp, octahedral voids \(=\) number of atoms \(= 3.613 \times 10^{23}\); tetrahedral voids \(= 2 \times\) atoms \(= 7.226 \times 10^{23}\). Total \(= 3.613 \times 10^{23} + 7.226 \times 10^{23} = 1.084 \times 10^{24}\). Matches option C.

89.subtopic: Types of Solutions, Solubility and Henry's Law
89.solution: Using Henry's law in the given form, concentration of dissolved gas \(= K_{H} \times P = 0.15\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{atm}^{-1} \times 0.15\,\text{atm} = 0.0225\,\text{mol dm}^{-3} = 0.0225\,\text{M}\). Matches option D.

90.solution: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained from the diet; histidine is one of them. Tyrosine, serine and glycine are non-essential (synthesised in the body). Matches option C.

91.solution: Molar mass of water \(= 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\). Mass of 0.25 mol \(= 0.25 \times 18 = 4.5\,\text{g}\). Matches option C.

92.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Alcohols and Acidity
92.solution: Sodium lauryl sulphate, \(\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{11}\text{OSO}_{3}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}\), is an anionic detergent (the surface-active part carries a negative charge). It is commonly used in toothpastes and shampoos. Matches option A.
92.note: Sodium lauryl sulphate is studied under detergents (cleansing agents). No dedicated 'detergents' subtopic exists in the taxonomy; filed under Alcohols/Ethers chapter's reactions as the closest available chemistry-of-cleansing-agents home. (Borderline classification.)

93.solution: Phloroglucinol is benzene-1,3,5-triol, i.e. a benzene ring with three \(-\text{OH}\) groups in the 1,3,5 (symmetric, alternate) positions. Option A shows exactly this symmetric 1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene. Option B is benzene-1,2,3-triol (pyrogallol), option C is benzene-1,2,4-triol (hydroxyhydroquinone), and option D is benzene-1,3-diol (resorcinol). Hence A is phloroglucinol. Matches option A.

optionOverrides.A: Benzene ring bearing three OH groups at positions 1, 3 and 5 (symmetric 1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene) — phloroglucinol.
optionOverrides.B: Benzene ring bearing three OH groups at positions 1, 2 and 3 (1,2,3-trihydroxybenzene) — pyrogallol.
optionOverrides.C: Benzene ring bearing three OH groups at positions 1, 2 and 4 (1,2,4-trihydroxybenzene) — hydroxyhydroquinone.
optionOverrides.D: Benzene ring bearing two OH groups at positions 1 and 3 (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) — resorcinol.

94.subtopic: Rate of Reaction, Stoichiometry and Average Rate
94.solution: For \(\text{N}_{2} + 3\text{H}_{2} \longrightarrow 2\text{NH}_{3}\), the rate is \(-\dfrac{d[\text{N}_{2}]}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{H}_{2}]}{dt} = +\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_{3}]}{dt}\). Equating the \(\text{H}_{2}\) and \(\text{NH}_{3}\) terms: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_{3}]}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{H}_{2}]}{dt}\), i.e. \(3\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_{3}]}{dt} = -2\dfrac{d[\text{H}_{2}]}{dt}\). Matches option D.

95.subtopic: Green Chemistry, Principles, Atom Economy and Green Solvents
95.solution: Percentage atom economy \(= \dfrac{\text{formula mass of desired product}}{\text{sum of formula masses of all reactants}} \times 100 = \dfrac{180}{138 + 102} \times 100 = \dfrac{180}{240} \times 100 = 75\%\). Matches option D.

96.solution: Lone pairs on the central atom: \(\text{NH}_{3}\) has 1; \(\text{SF}_{4}\) has 1 (\(\text{AB}_{4}\text{E}\)); \(\text{ICl}_{3}\) has 2 (\(\text{AB}_{3}\text{E}_{2}\), T-shaped); \(\text{PCl}_{3}\) has 1. The highest number of lone pairs (2) is in \(\text{ICl}_{3}\). Matches option C.

97.subtopic: Dipole Moment, Polarity and Intermolecular Forces
97.solution: Boiling point depends on intermolecular hydrogen bonding. \((\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5})_{2}\text{NH}\) (secondary amine) has N-H and can H-bond; \(n\text{-C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{OH}\) (alcohol) and \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}\) (acid, dimerises) H-bond strongly. \(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\) is a tertiary amine with no N-H, so it cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds and has the lowest boiling point. Matches option B.
97.note: Compares H-bonding (intermolecular forces) across compound classes; filed under Chemical Bonding > intermolecular forces (closest fit).

98.solution: In an fcc unit cell there are 4 atoms. Mass of one atom \(= \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-22}}{4} = 0.45 \times 10^{-22}\,\text{g}\). Molar mass \(=\) mass of one atom \(\times N_{A} = 0.45 \times 10^{-22} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 27.1\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\). Matches option A.

99.solution: Osmotic pressure \(\pi = \dfrac{n\,R\,T}{V} = \dfrac{0.03 \times 0.082 \times 300}{0.1} = \dfrac{0.738}{0.1} = 7.38 \approx 7.4\,\text{atm}\) (non-electrolyte, so \(i = 1\)). Matches option A.

100.subtopic: Bonding Theories, EAN, Crystal Field, Hybridization and Magnetism
100.solution: The Irving-Williams series gives the stability order of high-spin divalent first-row transition metal complexes with a given ligand: \(\text{Mn}^{2+} < \text{Fe}^{2+} < \text{Co}^{2+} < \text{Ni}^{2+} < \text{Cu}^{2+}\). Thus the decreasing-stability order among the listed ions is \(\text{Cu}^{2+} > \text{Mn}^{2+} > \text{Cd}^{2+}\). Matches option A.

101.solution: Rewrite as a linear ODE: \(x(x-1)\frac{dy}{dx}-(x-2)y=x^{3}(2x-1)\), i.e. \(\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{x-2}{x(x-1)}y=\frac{x^{2}(2x-1)}{x-1}\). With partial fractions \(\frac{2-x}{x(x-1)}=\frac{-2}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}\), the integrating factor is \(\text{I.F.}=e^{\int(-\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1})dx}=e^{-2\log x+\log(x-1)}=\frac{x-1}{x^{2}}\). Then \(y\cdot\frac{x-1}{x^{2}}=\int\frac{x-1}{x^{2}}\cdot\frac{x^{2}(2x-1)}{x-1}\,dx=\int(2x-1)\,dx=x^{2}-x+c\). Multiplying through by \(\frac{x^{2}}{x-1}\): \(y(x-1)=x^{2}(x^{2}-x)+cx^{2}=x^{3}(x-1)+cx^{2}\).

102.subtopic: Line — Equation, Direction Cosines, and Vector Form
102.solution: The line of intersection of two planes is along \(\bar{n}_{1}\times\bar{n}_{2}\), where \(\bar{n}_{1}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}\) and \(\bar{n}_{2}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}\). The cross product is \(\bar{n}_{1}\times\bar{n}_{2}=(-1-2)\hat{i}-(1-6)\hat{j}+(1+3)\hat{k}=-3\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+4\hat{k}\). Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{9+25+16}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}\). Hence the direction cosines are \(\frac{-3}{5\sqrt{2}},\frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}},\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}}\).

103.solution: Let the parts be \(x\) and \(20-x\), and maximise \(z=x^{3}(20-x)^{2}\). Then \(\frac{dz}{dx}=3x^{2}(20-x)^{2}+x^{3}\cdot 2(20-x)(-1)=x^{2}(20-x)[3(20-x)-2x]=x^{2}(20-x)(60-5x)\). Setting \(\frac{dz}{dx}=0\) gives \(x=12\) (rejecting \(x=0,20\)). The second-derivative test confirms a maximum at \(x=12\), so the parts are \(12\) and \(8\).

104.subtopic: Equation of Line — Rotation, Angle, and Bisector
104.solution: Diagonal \(AC\) joins \(A(2,-1)\) and \(C(2,3)\): it is vertical (slope \(=\infty\)). Diagonal \(BD\) joins \(B(0,2)\) and \(D(4,0)\): slope \(m=\frac{0-2}{4-0}=-\frac{1}{2}\). The acute angle a vertical line makes with a line of slope \(m\) is \(\theta\) with \(\tan\theta=\left|\frac{1}{m}\right|=2\). Hence \(\theta=\tan^{-1}2\).

105.subtopic: Tangent, Normal, Approximation, and Curve from Geometric Condition
105.solution: The shortest distance from the curve \(x=y^{2}\) to the line \(x-y+1=0\) (slope \(1\)) occurs where the tangent to the curve is parallel to the line. Differentiating \(x=y^{2}\): \(\frac{dx}{dy}=2y\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2y}=1\Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{2}\), \(x=\frac{1}{4}\). The point is \(\left(\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}\right)\). Distance \(=\frac{\left|\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}+1\right|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}=\frac{3/4}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{8}\).

106.subtopic: Equation of Circle from Diameter, Centre, and Concentric Conditions
106.solution: Factor the pair of lines: \(x^{2}-y^{2}-2x+4y-3=(x-1)^{2}-(y-2)^{2}=(x+y-3)(x-y+1)=0\). The two diameters are \(x+y=3\) and \(x-y=-1\); their intersection (the centre) is \((1,2)\). Since the circle passes through \((1,1)\), the radius is \(\sqrt{(1-1)^{2}+(2-1)^{2}}=1\). Equation: \((x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=1\).

108.solution: Normals are \((1,-2,3)\) and \((1,\alpha,2)\). With \(\cos\theta=\frac{1}{14}\): \(\frac{1-2\alpha+6}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{5+\alpha^{2}}}=\frac{1}{14}\), so \(14(7-2\alpha)=\sqrt{14}\sqrt{5+\alpha^{2}}\). Squaring: \(14(7-2\alpha)^{2}=5+\alpha^{2}\Rightarrow 55\alpha^{2}-392\alpha+681=0\). The difference between the two roots is \(\frac{\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{|a|}=\frac{\sqrt{392^{2}-4(55)(681)}}{55}=\frac{\sqrt{3844}}{55}=\frac{62}{55}\).

109.subtopic: Distance, Foot of Perpendicular, Projection, and Mirror Image
109.solution: Both lines have direction \(\bar{b}=(2,3,4)\), \(|\bar{b}|=\sqrt{29}\). With points \(\bar{a}_{1}=(k,4,3)\), \(\bar{a}_{2}=(2,4,7)\), \(\bar{a}_{2}-\bar{a}_{1}=(2-k,0,4)\). The shortest distance for parallel lines is \(\frac{|\bar{b}\times(\bar{a}_{2}-\bar{a}_{1})|}{|\bar{b}|}\). Compute \(\bar{b}\times(\bar{a}_{2}-\bar{a}_{1})=(12,\,-4k,\,3k-6)\), so \(\frac{\sqrt{144+16k^{2}+(3k-6)^{2}}}{\sqrt{29}}=\frac{13}{\sqrt{29}}\). Thus \(144+16k^{2}+(3k-6)^{2}=169\Rightarrow 25k^{2}-36k+11=0\Rightarrow k=1\) (or \(11/25\), and \(k=1\) is the listed value).

110.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
110.solution: The direction ratios are \((2,-4,1)\) and \((-1,2,3)\). \(\cos\theta=\left|\frac{(2)(-1)+(-4)(2)+(1)(3)}{\sqrt{4+16+1}\,\sqrt{1+4+9}}\right|=\left|\frac{-7}{\sqrt{21}\sqrt{14}}\right|=\frac{7}{7\sqrt{6}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\). Hence \(\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\right)\).

111.subtopic: Tangent, Normal, Approximation, and Curve from Geometric Condition
111.solution: For \(y^{2}=6x\): \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3}{y}\). For \(9x^{2}+by^{2}=16\): \(18x+2by\frac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{9x}{by}\). Orthogonality requires the product of slopes \(=-1\): \(\frac{3}{y}\cdot\left(-\frac{9x}{by}\right)=-1\Rightarrow\frac{27x}{by^{2}}=1\). Using \(y^{2}=6x\): \(\frac{27x}{b(6x)}=1\Rightarrow\frac{27}{6b}=1\Rightarrow b=\frac{9}{2}\).

112.solution: \(\sqrt{3}\cot20^{\circ}-4\cos20^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\cos20^{\circ}-4\sin20^{\circ}\cos20^{\circ}}{\sin20^{\circ}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\cos20^{\circ}-2\sin40^{\circ}}{\sin20^{\circ}}\). Writing \(\sqrt{3}\cos20^{\circ}=2\sin60^{\circ}\cos20^{\circ}=\sin80^{\circ}+\sin40^{\circ}\), the numerator becomes \(\sin80^{\circ}-\sin40^{\circ}=2\cos60^{\circ}\sin20^{\circ}=\sin20^{\circ}\). Hence the value is \(\frac{\sin20^{\circ}}{\sin20^{\circ}}=1\).

113.solution: With \(|\bar a|=1,|\bar b|=4,\bar a\cdot\bar b=2\): \(|\bar a\times\bar b|^{2}=|\bar a|^{2}|\bar b|^{2}-(\bar a\cdot\bar b)^{2}=16-4=12\). For \(\bar c=2(\bar a\times\bar b)-3\bar b\), since \(\bar b\cdot(\bar a\times\bar b)=0\), \(|\bar c|^{2}=4(12)+9(16)=192\). Also \(\bar b\cdot\bar c=2\bar b\cdot(\bar a\times\bar b)-3|\bar b|^{2}=-48\). Then \(\cos\theta=\frac{\bar b\cdot\bar c}{|\bar b||\bar c|}=\frac{-48}{4\cdot 8\sqrt{3}}=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}\), giving \(\theta=\frac{5\pi}{6}\).

114.solution: \([\bar a\bar b\bar d]\bar c-[\bar a\bar b\bar c]\bar d=((\bar a\times\bar b)\cdot\bar d)\bar c-((\bar a\times\bar b)\cdot\bar c)\bar d=(\bar a\times\bar b)\times(\bar c\times\bar d)\). Hence value \(=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{8}\).

121.solution: In the first quadrant the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{4}=1\) gives \(y=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9-x^{2}}\). Quarter-ellipse area \(=\int_{0}^{3}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9-x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{9}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{3\pi}{2}\). The line \(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{y}{2}=1\) and the axes form a triangle of area \(\frac{1}{2}(3)(2)=3\). Required area between ellipse arc and line \(=\frac{3\pi}{2}-3=\frac{3}{2}(\pi-2)\) sq. units.

122.subtopic: Continuity at a Point — Finding Parameters
122.solution: Continuity at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\) requires the left and right limits to be equal: \(m\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}+1=\sin\frac{\pi}{2}+n=1+n\). Hence \(\frac{m\pi}{2}=n\), i.e. \(n=\frac{m\pi}{2}\).

123.solution: \(x^{2}-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)\) is negative on \((-1,2)\) and positive on \([-2,-1]\). So \(\int_{-2}^{2}|x^{2}-x-2|dx=\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^{2}-x-2)dx+\int_{-1}^{2}-(x^{2}-x-2)dx\). Evaluating, the first integral \(=\frac{11}{6}\) and the second \(=\frac{27}{6}\)... computing precisely gives a total of \(\frac{19}{3}\).

124.solution: \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{\tan x}-e^{x}}{\tan x-x}=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}(e^{\tan x-x}-1)}{\tan x-x}\). As \(x\to 0\), \(\tan x-x\to 0\) and \(\frac{e^{u}-1}{u}\to 1\) with \(u=\tan x-x\), while \(e^{x}\to 1\). Hence the limit is \(1\cdot 1=1\).

125.solution: For \(x^{2}=20y\), \(4a=20\Rightarrow a=5\); vertex \((0,0)\), focus \((0,5)\). The latus rectum has length \(4a=20\) with endpoints \((-10,5)\) and \((10,5)\). The triangle formed with the vertex has base \(20\) and height \(5\): area \(=\frac{1}{2}\times 20\times 5=50\) sq. units.

126.solution: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{1+x+x^{2}}-\sqrt{1-x+x^{2}}\). Then \(f(-x)=\sqrt{1-x+x^{2}}-\sqrt{1+x+x^{2}}=-f(x)\), so \(f\) is odd. The integral of an odd function over the symmetric interval \([-1,1]\) is \(0\).

127.subtopic: Basic Probability — Events, Conditional, and Complement
127.solution: From \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) with replacement, total outcomes \(=16\). Count pairs with \(p^{2}\ge 4q\): for \(p=2\) (\(p^{2}=4\)): \(q=1\) (1 case); \(p=3\) (\(9\ge 4q\Rightarrow q\le 2.25\)): \(q=1,2\) (2 cases); \(p=4\) (\(16\ge 4q\Rightarrow q\le 4\)): \(q=1,2,3,4\) (4 cases); \(p=1\): none. Total favourable \(=7\). Probability \(=\frac{7}{16}\).

128.solution: For \(f(x)=\frac{2x+3}{3x+4}\): assuming \(f(x_{1})=f(x_{2})\) leads to \((2x_{1}+3)(3x_{2}+4)=(2x_{2}+3)(3x_{1}+4)\Rightarrow x_{1}=x_{2}\), so \(f\) is one-one. Solving \(y=\frac{2x+3}{3x+4}\) for \(x\) gives \(x=\frac{3-4y}{3y-2}\), valid for all \(y\) except \(y=\frac{2}{3}\). Hence \(f\) is one-one and onto for \(y\neq\frac{2}{3}\).

130.solution: Partial fractions: \(\frac{2x+3}{(x-1)(x^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^{2}+1}\) gives \(A=\frac{5}{2},B=-\frac{5}{2},C=-\frac{1}{2}\). Integrating: \(\frac{5}{2}\log(x-1)-\frac{5}{4}\log(x^{2}+1)-\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x+A=\log\{(x-1)^{5/2}(x^{2}+1)^{-5/4}\}-\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x+A\). Comparing the exponent of \((x^{2}+1)\) gives \(a=-\frac{5}{4}\).

131.solution: Continuous compounding (or the equivalent ratio model): \(400\) doubles to \(800\) in \(6\) years, so the growth factor per year is \(2^{1/6}\). After \(33\) years, amount \(=400\cdot 2^{33/6}=400\cdot 2^{5.5}=400\cdot 32\cdot\sqrt{2}=400\cdot 32\cdot 1.4142=18101.76\).

141.solution: Using the cosine rule \(\cos A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc}\) etc., the given relation \(\frac{2\cos A}{a}+\frac{\cos B}{b}+\frac{2\cos C}{c}=\frac{a}{bc}+\frac{b}{ca}\) simplifies (multiplying through by \(2abc\)) to \(2(b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2})+(a^{2}+c^{2}-b^{2})+2(a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2})=2a^{2}+2b^{2}\), which reduces to \(a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}\). Thus the triangle is right-angled at \(A\): \(\angle A=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
